findings.source_passage: this seems so outlandish a thing that one must needs go a little into the history and philosophy of it.
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'history and philosophy of it' is a characteristic Ishmael register-setter, signaling the mock-scholarly digressive mode that governs the whole chapter; its replacement with '—outlandish, yet historical' strips the ironic framing.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'one must needs go a little into the history and philosophy of it' to close the opening sentence.

findings.source_passage: The old monks of Dunfermline were very fond of them. They had a great porpoise grant from the crown.
findings.why_it_matters: The monks-of-Dunfermline detail is a prime example of Melville's deadpan antiquarian wit; its two-sentence rhythm is stylistically distinctive and the 'porpoise grant from the crown' is a comic punch-line that defines the chapter's mock-erudite voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Reinsert the two sentences about the monks of Dunfermline and their crown porpoise grant after the porpoise-balls detail.

findings.source_passage: They have such an eatable look that the most self-denying stranger can hardly keep his hands off.
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is the comic pay-off of the Amsterdam doughnuts riff; without it the fritters passage ends flatly on description rather than on the ironic appetitive joke that is Melville's point.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the closing sentence about the eatable look of the fritters after the oly-cooks comparison.

findings.source_passage: Many a good supper have I thus made.
findings.why_it_matters: This first-person intrusion—'Many a good supper have I thus made'—is an important voice marker, pulling the narrator into personal participation in the chapter's theme and grounding the chapter's abstractions in lived experience.
findings.suggested_fix: Append 'Many a good supper have I thus made.' to the ship-biscuit sentence.

findings.source_passage: every one knows that some young bucks among the epicures, by continually dining upon calves' brains, by and by get to have a little brains of their own, so as to be able to tell a calf's head from their own heads; which, indeed, requires uncommon discrimination. And that is the reason why a young buck with an intelligent looking calf's head before him, is somehow one of the saddest sights you can see.
findings.why_it_matters: This sustained satirical aside—the joke about epicures acquiring brains from calves' brains, culminating in 'one of the saddest sights you can see'—is a fully developed comic digression; its loss reduces the paragraph to bare fact and cuts directly to the 'Et tu Brute!' punchline without its proper build-up.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full joke about young bucks dining on calves' brains and the saddest-sights observation before the 'Et tu Brute!' line.

summary: The draft preserves the chapter's major argumentative arc and most famous passages intact, but systematically strips the mid-paragraph comic digressions and voice-establishing asides—monks of Dunfermline, the fritters pay-off, 'Many a good supper have I thus made,' and the calves'-brains joke—producing five medium-severity voice-flattening losses that collectively hollow out the chapter's mock-scholarly satirical register.
